config.prompt: File each law by its order — the highest derivative it contains:

items.label: F = ma = m·x″ — Newton's second law

config.why: Order is the highest derivative present: one derivative for first order, two for second. Every mechanics problem built on F = ma is second order; every 'rate proportional to…' law is first.

activities.anchor: Bacteria in a flask, adopters of a technology
activities.caption: call the growth rate at P = 2
activities.name: deRateEst

config.prompt: A logistic population obeys dP/dt = 0.4·P·(1 − P/10). At P = 2, what is dP/dt?
config.why: 0.4 × 2 × (1 − 0.2) = 0.64 per year. The same law peaks at half the carrying capacity, where dP/dt = k·pₘₐₓ/4 = 1 per year.
config.context: the S-curve is steepest at P = pₘₐₓ/2, not at the start

activities.caption: fill the blanks — one formula, growth and decay
activities.name: deHalfLifeCloze

config.text: With P = P₀·e^(kt), the doubling time is T = ln 2 / k ≈ %%0%% / k — the rule of 70 when k is a percentage. Radioactive decay uses the same formula with k negative: at k = −0.01 per year the half-life is about %%1%% years.
config.hint: ln 2 ≈ 0.693, and the half-life is the same calculation with |k|.

config.prompt: Coffee at 90 °C cools in a 20 °C room with k = 0.07 per minute. What is its temperature after 20 minutes?
config.why: Excess temperature 70·e^(−1.4) ≈ 17.3 °C above room, so T ≈ 37.3 °C. After 30 minutes the excess is only 8.6 °C.
config.context: the excess halves roughly every 10 minutes (ln 2 / 0.07 ≈ 9.9 min)

activities.anchor: Standard example, the charging RC circuit
activities.caption: rebuild the integrating-factor solution
activities.name: deRcOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the integrating-factor solution of dq/dt + q/(RC) = V/R:
items: Write the equation in standard form: dq/dt + q/(RC) = V/R
Identify p(t) = 1/(RC) and build μ = e^(t/RC)
Multiply through; the left side collapses to d/dt (q·e^(t/RC))
Integrate both sides: q·e^(t/RC) = CV·e^(t/RC) + K
Apply q(0) = 0, giving q(t) = CV(1 − e^(−t/RC))
config.why: The integrating factor is chosen to reverse the product rule: μq′ + μp·q = (μq)′. The initial condition then fixes the one remaining constant.

activities.anchor: Newton's F = ma makes every mechanics problem
activities.caption: pair each spring with its frequency
activities.name: deOmegaMatch

config.prompt: Pair each mass–spring system with its natural angular frequency ω = √(k/m):
config.why: ω = √(k/m). Stiffness raises the frequency as its square root; mass lowers it the same way — which is why a heavy bell rings low.

config.root: A mass on a spring is set oscillating. You increase the damping c from zero. Trace what happens.

start.text: At c = 0 the mass oscillates forever. As damping c rises from zero, which change happens first?

choices.label: The amplitude decays but the mass still oscillates
choices.feedback: This is the underdamped regime: sine waves inside a shrinking exponential envelope.

choices.label: The mass stops oscillating at once
choices.feedback: Damping removes energy gradually; oscillation persists until the critical value.

choices.label: The oscillation frequency rises
choices.feedback: Damping actually lowers the frequency slightly.

under.text: Underdamped. Keep raising c. What is special about the boundary case where oscillation just disappears?

choices.label: It returns to rest faster than any other non-oscillating case
choices.feedback: Yes: critically damped is the fastest possible return without overshoot.

choices.label: It is the slowest non-oscillating case
choices.feedback: No: past the boundary the return gets slower, not faster.

critical.text: Critical damping — the knife-edge. Shock absorbers are tuned here because it settles in minimum time without bouncing.

over.text: Overdamped — no oscillation, but a sluggish return. A soft door closer behaves this way.

sudden.text: It still oscillates at first; only at the critical damping value does overshoot vanish.

choices.label: Continue
choices.feedback: Follow the decaying oscillation into the boundary case.

freq.text: The damped frequency is slightly lower than the natural frequency, not higher.

config.why: Three regimes: underdamped oscillates with decaying amplitude; critically damped returns fastest without overshoot; overdamped returns slowly without oscillating.

activities.anchor: is a value where the rate is zero
activities.caption: mark the stable equilibrium
activities.name: deEquilPlace

config.prompt: The logistic law dP/dt = 0.4·P·(1 − P/10) has equilibria at P = 0 and P = 10. Place the stable one on the axis.
config.why: P = 10 is stable — below it the rate is positive, above it negative, so arrows on the phase line point toward it. P = 0 is unstable.

activities.caption: true or false — what Euler does and does not promise
activities.name: deEulerJudge

statements.s: Euler's method samples the slope at the start of each step, so for y′ = y it systematically undershoots the true curve.
statements.why: The true slope keeps rising across the step; every step uses a slightly too-small slope.

statements.s: Halving the step size halves the error, which makes Euler's method second-order accurate.
statements.why: Halving h halves the error only for first-order methods — and that is exactly what Euler is; second-order methods reduce error by about a factor of four.

statements.s: If a numerical solution disagrees with experiment, the cause must be integration error.
statements.why: The equation itself may omit friction, delays or stochasticity — model error and integration error are different suspects.

activities.caption: exact formula versus numerical solution — drag the divider
activities.name: deExactCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to answer a differential equation — drag the divider:

before.label: symbolic
before.text: Separation and integrating factors give an exact formula — but only for the small family of equations that cooperate.

after.label: numerical
after.text: Euler and Runge–Kutta give approximate values — but they apply to the three-body problem, weather and Navier–Stokes.

config.why: Closed forms are the exception, not the rule; numerics is the general method, and its error can be measured and shrunk.
